💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that elisa Seghetti is Co-Founder and CEO of Saturn Dynamics, with a background spanning biotech, computational chemistry, and enterprise AI.
  • According to recent reports, saturn Dynamics develops physics-based world models for robotics and embodied AI.
  • After scaling AiGot’s enterprise AI business, what gap in robotics training led you to co-found Saturn Dynamics and pursue a physics-based world model?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that elisa Seghetti is Co-Founder and CEO of Saturn Dynamics, with a background spanning biotech, computational chemistry, and enterprise AI. She previously founded AiGot, growing its engineering team from three to more than 35 people and working with Fortune 500 companies on their AI strategies. Her focus at Saturn Dynamics is helping physical AI learn to operate safely and reliably alongside people.

According to recent reports, saturn Dynamics develops physics-based world models for robotics and embodied AI. Its Arc model creates interactive simulated environments where robotics teams can generate training data, explore variations in physical tasks, and evaluate control policies before carrying out experiments on real hardware.

After scaling AiGot’s enterprise AI business, what gap in robotics training led you to co-found Saturn Dynamics and pursue a physics-based world model?

Industry observers note that I founded AiGot in 2021 to help businesses use AI to automate complex processes. As we scaled the tech giant and worked with Fortune 500 businesses, I saw first-hand the challenges of making AI reliable in real-world environments: lack of data, misaligned expectations, hype. But I also began to see a newly introduced opportunity emerging. AI would not be confined to screens forever; increasingly, it would be interacting with the physical world. Having spent years building AI that enterprises could trust, I sought to apply that experience to a new challenge: developing better ways to train physical AI to operate safely and reliably side by side with humans. That led me to co-found Saturn Dynamics and pursue a physics-based world model.

According to recent reports, today, much of robotics training relies on video-based learning and egocentric data collection, with people wearing cameras to capture demonstrations of everyday tasks. While this provides valuable data, it is expensive and time-consuming to collect at scale, and watching an action doesn’t necessarily teach a robot how to replicate it or understand its physical consequences.

We saw an opportunity to move beyond learning through observation alone, giving robots an interactive environment to learn through trial and error without relying entirely on real-world data collection.

For readers unfamiliar with world models, how would you explain how a robot learns a task using Arc?

A world model is essentially a model that learns how the world behaves and how it changes in response to different actions.

Imagine you are training a robot to move a tyre along a factory production line. You could show it thousands of videos of the task, but that doesn’t necessarily teach it how much force to apply, how the tyre will respond if it slips, or how its approach should change if the tyre is heavier than expected.

We have created Arc, a world model that allows robotics teams to place physical AI in an interactive simulation where it can try different approaches, observe the predicted outcomes and improve its next attempt. It can rapidly explore multiple scenarios in parallel, testing different actions without having to carry out every experiment on physical hardware. This allows teams to test potentially risky situations without risking damage to equipment or putting people working on the factory floor in harm’s way.

How does embedding mathematical symmetries and physical principles into Arc distinguish it from conventional simulators and video-based world models?

According to recent reports, the physical world is governed by mathematical relationships that remain consistent across different environments. At Saturn Dynamics, our team combines expertise in theoretical physics, reinforcement learning and machine learning to build these principles directly into Arc’s architecture and training approach.

It has been revealed that conventional physics simulators typically rely on engineers defining the environment and specifying the physical properties and parameters that govern how objects behave. While this can produce highly accurate simulations, configuring and adapting them to different scenarios can require a lot of work. Video-based world models, meanwhile, are more time and cost effective but visual data does not always reveal the underlying physical principles governing an object’s behaviour.

A key part of Arc’s approach is mathematical symmetry. In physics, symmetries describe properties that remain unchanged when a system is transformed, such as moving an object to a different position or rotating it. By incorporating these relationships into Arc, the model can recognise how the underlying rules of physics apply across different situations, rather than having to learn them repeatedly from data and as a result, the computational cost is far lower.

How does Arc learn physical properties such as weight, friction, and flexibility that cannot always be determined from images alone?

Our world model is trained on multiple modalities of data, not only images or video. We also feed it physical information, such as depth and force, which helps Arc understand how objects respond to physical interactions. By learning from both visual information and these physical measurements, the model can develop an understanding of physical behaviours that extends beyond the specific examples in its training data. For example, when running experiments where most of Arc’s training data involved rigid objects, we actually observed that the model was able to learn how to simulate how softer, more flexible objects bend and change shape when handled.

How were the benchmarks behind Arc’s reported speed and trajectory accuracy advantages over NVIDIA’s Cosmos models designed?

We designed the benchmarks to evaluate two key aspects of a world model’s performance: how accurately it predicts the physical world, and how efficiently it can generate simulation data.

In the benchmark, we tracked and measured the movements generated by the world model. We checked the accuracy of this process by calibrating against real-world robotics data and simulation data. We then tested the model using two types of movements: real-world robot movements, to assess how accurately it could reproduce familiar actions, and more complex, artificially created movements to test how well it could handle a wider range of possible movements, including those it may not have encountered before.

We evaluated Arc against NVIDIA’s Cosmos world models, Cosmos Nano and Cosmos Edge. In this test, Arc achieved 73% greater trajectory accuracy than Cosmos Nano.

Sources indicate that we also evaluated how quickly each model could generate simulation data. We ran multiple benchmarks on different hardware from low-power deployment devices like NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor to high-end high-power GPUs such as NVIDIA’s B200. To ensure a fair comparison, we ran hundreds of generations under the same conditions. On an NVIDIA Jetson Thor, Arc generated one second of simulation data in 0.6 seconds, compared with 23 seconds for Cosmos Nano and nine seconds for Cosmos Edge, making it faster than real time. These benchmarks show that Arc can deliver greater trajectory accuracy and faster data generation than the models we tested against.

What evidence can you share that skills learned with Arc transfer successfully to physical robots?

In a recent development, for example, in an automotive kitting use case we are evaluating with a leading automotive OEM, a robot repeatedly struggled to grasp an awkwardly shaped component. Using Arc to generate thousands of practice runs, we exposed the policy to different ways of approaching and handling the component, helping it adapt to real-world variability and reliably complete the grasp without weeks of tuning on the factory floor.

The resulting policies can then be evaluated against actual production requirements, including cycle time, task success and intervention frequency, before being tested on physical robots.

How do you prevent robots from learning to exploit inaccuracies in Arc’s simulations?

One of the key challenges in robotics is the sim-to-real gap: the difference between how a robot behaves in a simulated environment and how it performs in the physical world. A robot may learn to complete a task in simulation by exploiting inaccuracies in the model, only to find that the same approach fails when deployed on real hardware.

According to recent reports, we address this by combining real-world and synthetic training data, rather than relying on simulation alone. Real-world data helps ground the robot’s learning in actual physical behaviour, while synthetic data gives it more opportunities to practise. As we collect more data from factories to improve Arc, its simulations become increasingly accurate, allowing us to generate more realistic training data and reduce reliance on real-world data collection.

Can you walk us through a customer or pilot example that illustrates how Arc fits into an existing robotics training pipeline?

Saturn Dynamics uses its world model to train robotics policies, either by generating synthetic training data or using the model as a backbone for the policy itself, known as a world action model.

This can help robots tackle difficult real-world tasks where they might otherwise struggle with unexpected variations. One example is industrial kitting, where a robot must pick different components from bins and assemble kits within strict production cycle times, accounting for variations in component position, shape and weight while maintaining a consistent success rate.

In a recent development, in a conventional workflow, robotics teams collect hundreds of hours of human demonstrations, train a control policy and repeatedly test it on physical hardware. This process is slow and expensive. Arc accelerates this pipeline by generating thousands of simulated execution scenarios from task-specific observations and robot actions, introducing variations in factors such as approach angles, surface grips and component orientations.

Our objective is to make existing robotics development pipelines faster and more scalable, without requiring customers to replace their hardware, collect data through human demonstrations or rebuild their entire software stack.

Where do you see Saturn Dynamics’ strongest competitive advantage in an ecosystem that includes NVIDIA and established simulation platforms?

In a recent development, our focus is on making high-quality simulation scalable and economically viable for robotics teams. Training robots requires vast amounts of data, and generating that data through simulation can become a significant bottleneck in terms of compute, time and cost.

Our benchmarks show that Arc can generate data faster than the NVIDIA Cosmos models we tested against, while using a fraction of the compute and cost. This means robotics teams can explore more scenarios, run more experiments and generate more training data without the same computational burden. We see this as a key step towards making large-scale robotics training more accessible.

Sources indicate that there is also a wider opportunity for Europe. While the US and China took the lead in the first wave of commercial AI, Europe’s industrial heritage gives it a distinct advantage in physical AI. As regions look to reduce their reliance on foreign technology, we believe making robotics training more scalable and cost-efficient can help European companies develop their own capabilities and compete in this next wave of AI innovation.

What milestone would demonstrate that Arc is helping robotics move beyond compelling demonstrations into reliable everyday use?

Our North Star has always been having robot deployments that are reliable, safe and scalable. Going past benchmarks and demos, the core milestone is when a robot can carry out a useful task across full production shifts, handle the variations that naturally occur on a factory floor and require very few human interventions.

In a recent development, A successful demonstration tells you very little about whether a system is ready for deployment. We need to measure sustained task success, cycle time, uptime, interventions per hour and, ultimately, whether the economics work for the customer.

From a commercial perspective, the milestone is when successful pilots consistently turn into larger fleet deployments, with a clear payback period for customers.

Just as importantly, we want to see the same training and evaluation process work across multiple tasks, robot platforms and production sites without starting from scratch every time.

That is when robotics becomes scalable: when deploying the next robot requires progressively less engineering effort than deploying the first.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore generative simulation and world models for training and evaluating robotics systems should visit Saturn Dynamics.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the fresh US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post highlights you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

It has been revealed that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

In a recent development, if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Sources indicate that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

It has been revealed that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Recent findings suggest that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

According to recent reports, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

In a recent development, only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Sources indicate that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Industry observers note that hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

According to recent reports, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

In a recent development, beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Recent findings suggest that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Recent findings suggest that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Sources indicate that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Sources indicate that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

According to recent reports, the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Sources indicate that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can enhancement the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Enhancement: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Sources indicate that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one patch behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Industry observers note that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Industry observers note that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot demonstrates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

In a recent development, decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

Recent findings suggest that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Industry observers note that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Sources indicate that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

In a recent development, written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style enhancement costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

Recent findings suggest that for every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all owners. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 sx prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional @primer/styled-react package let sx keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:.

Industry observers note that A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

Sources indicate that on Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not big enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

In a recent development, gitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

The Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic reported on November 25, 2026 that Claude agents helped move its Messages API from Python to Rust without an outage or a freeze on feature development.
  • Industry observers note that built in Python in 2023, the Messages API is the primary route through which customers and Anthropic apps such as Claude Code and Cowork reach Claude.
  • Sources indicate that an initial rewrite of model-output parsing in Rust cut CPU usage by about 8% to 10%, Anthropic reports, but each token then crossed between Python and Rust three times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic reported on November 25, 2026 that Claude agents helped move its Messages API from Python to Rust without an outage or a freeze on feature development. Per-request CPU and memory use fell about 70% and more than 80%, respectively, while the median wait for the first response token fell about 20% for customers’ Claude Code requests.

Industry observers note that built in Python in 2023, the Messages API is the primary route through which customers and Anthropic apps such as Claude Code and Cowork reach Claude. Anthropic claims API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times from early 2024 to fall 2026. By late 2025, Python was adding overhead throughout an expanding sequence of request and response processing each time it created an object, freed memory or handed work to the next task.

Sources indicate that an initial rewrite of model-output parsing in Rust cut CPU usage by about 8% to 10%, Anthropic reports, but each token then crossed between Python and Rust three times. The team concluded that the savings did not justify the added overhead and complexity.

It has been revealed that claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week, according to Anthropic. The full rewrite covered both the input and output paths around the model. Because the Python service continued changing, generating replacement code was only the start: the team still had to demonstrate behavioral parity with a moving production system.

The existing suite had about 700 integration tests, but those tests were coupled to the Python implementation and covered only a subset of possible feature combinations. Claude helped change both the tests and the code, so a passing result could reflect a weakened check rather than correct behavior; an audit found more than 100 weakened assertions.

The Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April 2026, Anthropic reports, yet only about a quarter of compared production inputs matched Python. Production traffic also exposed how often a bug actually fired, whereas each test case counts only once. A single common bug could therefore account for many mismatches even when the test suite looked healthy.

The team made the live Python service its reference, then compared how the two implementations handled the same production requests. Because Claude can respond nondeterministically to identical input, the model ran once and its output was replayed to Rust. The comparisons covered processing on both sides of the model call, including request validation, prompt construction, tokenization, safety classification, output streaming and usage counting. The design also ensured that a request counted only once toward a customer’s usage limits and bill.

To protect customer content, engineers worked without reading requests or Claude’s replies. Instead of storing text, checkpointing located the first processing step or prompt component where the versions diverged. A fingerprint added the first differing position and the length difference, enabling records likely caused by the same bug to be grouped.

It has been revealed that A script processed new records every 10 to 30 minutes and alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it found a new kind. The coordinator assigned worker agents and opened shared Slack threads where engineers could follow and steer their work.

Worker agents ran in cloud sandboxes containing both codebases. Local checks could compare input processing in under a second without calling the model, Anthropic notes; a later output check passed scripted replies through both versions using a fake model. Because an agent could see only the fingerprint, it generated its own request or model reply to reproduce the mismatch. Once its edit made the versions agree, it added a regression test that failed on the old code and passed on the fixed code.

Engineers reviewed each proposed pull request before a fix could enter the slower outer loop, which compared shadowed production traffic on deployments with and without the change. Differences that persisted returned to the inner loop.

Industry observers note that in mid-May 2026, an agent proposed copying a missing web-search tool description into files. That made the prompts match and satisfied the local verifier, but an engineer rejected the workaround because Rust still needed to call the internal service supplying the description before launch. The episode exposed the limit of the automated signal: it could judge whether outputs matched, while engineers still had to judge whether a fix was durable enough to ship.

A memory loop preserved those judgments. The rejected shortcut became a note explaining the required service call, helping agents link later fingerprints to the known bug rather than devise another workaround. Other review lessons became porting rules, regression tests and lints; a later merge check required any Python change to be mirrored in Rust or receive an exemption.

It has been revealed that the post’s chart records the compared-input match rate reaching 99.6% by August 2026, with the qualification that what was compared changed over time, beginning on Anthropic’s own traffic before moving to a wider sample. Public traffic moved to Rust in September 2026.

It has been revealed that agents chose hypotheses, reproduction methods and fixes, while engineers increasingly supplied reviews and the rules and checks around them. The project connects infrastructure efficiency to a broader requirement for agentic development: production behavior must become a signal agents can act on, with human judgment applied to the shipping decisions that signal cannot settle.

His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a fresh native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a fresh native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Sources indicate that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Sources indicate that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

It has been revealed that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Industry observers note that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Industry observers note that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

It has been revealed that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

It has been revealed that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Recent findings suggest that parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Sources indicate that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

In a recent development, many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

In a recent development, more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Industry observers note that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, people can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

  • Industry observers note that the goal is to enable robots to acquire new skills by observing humans and other machines.
  • In a recent development, one of the most interesting developments in this area comes from NVIDIA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that egocentric videos remain an crucial source of training data for robots. But researchers are looking beyond this approach, exploring how robots can learn from third-person demonstrations and the experiences of other robotic systems.

Industry observers note that the goal is to enable robots to acquire new skills by observing humans and other machines. But how close are we to making this a reality, and what technical challenges still stand in the way?

In a recent development, one of the most interesting developments in this area comes from NVIDIA. The company developed NVIDIA Cosmos, a platform for building Physical AI models, and introduced Cosmos 3 in 2026. The model can interpret what is happening in a video, understand spatial relationships between objects, and predict the outcomes of specific actions.

According to recent reports, but understanding a video is only part of the challenge. A camera positioned in front of a person does not capture the same view as the person performing the task. Some movements and objects may be hidden from view, so training a robot requires reconstructing the spatial relationships between the person, the tools they use, and the surrounding environment.

In a recent development, this is the challenge NVIDIA is addressing with Grounded-Exo2Ego, a technology introduced in August 2026. It converts third-person footage into videos that show the scene from the perspective of the person performing the task. To do this, the system combines 3D scene reconstruction with semantic understanding of objects, enabling it to reconstruct parts of the scene that were not visible to the original camera. Demonstrations include cooking, performing CPR, and repairing a bicycle.

Industry observers note that for now, Grounded-Exo2Ego does not teach robots to perform the actions they observe. The model generates video rather than a sequence of commands that a robot can execute. It also has to make assumptions about parts of the scene that are hidden from view. Even so, the technology could make third-person footage a more useful source of training data for robotics.

The next step is translating observed actions into movements that robots can actually perform, given that their physical capabilities differ from those of humans.

Industry observers note that in November 2026, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, a model designed to predict future states of the environment and a robot’s actions. Its pretraining involved more than 400,000 hours of egocentric video, demonstrations recorded using handheld gripper devices, and footage of teleoperated robots. Unlike Grounded-Exo2Ego, this technology is specifically designed to control robotic systems.

In one experiment, a robot equipped with two five-fingered hands was tasked with placing filter paper into a funnel and wetting it with liquid. The robot had previously seen only human demonstrations of the task, with no examples of it being performed by the robot itself. It achieved a 65% success rate. In another experiment, a robotic arm assembled a toy dump truck using demonstrations recorded with a different gripper type, achieving a 60% success rate.

Recent findings suggest that I have little doubt that robots will eventually be able to learn new tasks by watching humans and other machines. NVIDIA’s research is already showing promising results, although these are still individual experiments rather than technologies deployed at scale. To me, the next major step is enabling robots to share what they have learned with one another. Could robots build on each other’s experience without having to go through the entire training process every time?

Industry observers note that transferring skills between robots introduces new challenges in validating what they have learned. If one robotic arm can learn to grip and move objects successfully, there is no guarantee that another robot will replicate this ability with the same precision. The outcome depends on the gripper design, the characteristics of the objects, the arrangement of the equipment, and the conditions in the working environment.

If that experience is used to enhancement a shared model, validation becomes even more important. We need to assess how reliably a fresh skill performs across different robots, identify the conditions under which errors occur, and determine whether an update can be safely deployed to other machines. And successfully completing a task does not necessarily mean the system has chosen a safe way to achieve the result.

The complexity of validation is already evident in the preparation of training data. For example, in one of the projects of Keymakr involving robots that automate meal assembly, the team had to label transparent containers whose edges were almost indistinguishable from the background. They also had to determine which ingredients a robotic gripper could physically grasp. Some tasks required comparing images taken before and after ingredients were moved, while ambiguous cases underwent additional review. As upcoming scenarios emerged, the annotation guidelines were refined. The project ultimately achieved 98.65% annotation accuracy.

According to recent reports, in this case, the specialists were responsible for validating the quality of the training data. With collective learning, that responsibility would extend to evaluating how robots apply acquired skills in real-world conditions. For instance, we would need to verify whether a robot can handle objects of different shapes or adapt to changes in their positions, without creating safety risks.

I believe human validation will remain essential for at least another 15 years. Even if robots become capable of learning new tasks independently, someone will still need to verify that they are performing those tasks correctly.

It has been revealed that the ability to transfer skills between robots has clear practical implications for manufacturing. If one robot learns a new task and its experience can be validated and used to train others, manufacturers could adapt their production processes much faster, without having to train every machine individually.

It has been revealed that modern factories already demonstrate just how efficient robotic systems can be. In March 2026, for example, Chinese automaker GAC reported that its smart AION factory produces a latest vehicle every 53 seconds. More than 600 industrial robots operate in its welding workshop, while the factory can manufacture up to ten vehicle models with over 100,000 possible configurations.

Recent findings suggest that but a high level of automation does not mean robots can learn new tasks on their own. The next stage of industrial development will depend on how easily manufacturers can adapt their equipment to changing production needs.

Toyota offers an interesting example of this shift. In November 2026, the organization declared looks to establish Toyota Robotics, a dedicated division responsible for developing, deploying, and commercializing robotic systems, starting in January 2027. The scale of its ambitions is significant. Toyota estimates that the Toyota Group and its suppliers may need around 400,000 robots between 2028 and 2040. Eventually, the company also plans to offer its robotic solutions to other industries.

At the same time, Toyota’s leadership recognizes that simply increasing the number of robots is not enough. During a November investor meeting, manufacturer Vice President Yoichi Miyazaki pointed out that to deliver meaningful economic benefits, a robot that presently performs a single task would need to be capable of handling three or four tasks.

This is where collective learning could make a real difference. If robots can learn from one another, manufacturers would no longer have to start the training process from scratch every time production requirements change. Of course, there are still major challenges to overcome, particularly around hardware compatibility and skill validation. But in the long run, a robot’s value may be measured not only by what it can do, but also by how quickly another robot can learn from it.

Industry observers note that the high cost of developing and deploying AI and robotic systems is a subject of considerable debate today. Building hardware, training models, integrating systems into production processes, and maintaining them over time all require substantial investment. But today’s costs tell us little about how much these technologies might cost in a few years.

Historically, many technological breakthroughs have followed a similar path. First comes disruption: a new solution emerges that fundamentally changes how a particular task is approached. At this stage, companies focus their resources primarily on making the technology work. Once its capabilities have been proven in practice, the focus shifts to optimization. Developers start looking for ways to reduce costs, improve performance, and scale the product.

Sources indicate that in my project, Scryon, collecting and processing information about a single professional conference initially cost hundreds of dollars and took about six hours of my time. After we automated and optimised the process, both the cost and the time required fell significantly.

I expect robotics to follow a similar trajectory, although optimization will be more challenging because of the physical hardware involved, safety requirements, and ongoing maintenance. Investors are presently pouring money into Physical AI, and companies are introducing new technologies, but many of these developments are still being tested. It will take several years for many of today’s projects to evolve into products ready for full-scale deployment.

What I find particularly interesting is how the ability to share skills between robots could change the economics of deployment. Today, teaching a robot a new task may require additional demonstrations, configuration, and testing. If one robot masters a task and hundreds of others can benefit from that experience, the cost of training each additional machine could fall significantly. There would still be costs associated with adapting and validating those skills, of course.

Industry observers note that I would measure the success of these technologies using a few practical metrics: how long it takes a robot to learn a new task, how consistently it performs that task, and how much it costs to transfer that skill to other machines. These are the measures that will ultimately tell us whether collective learning can truly transform the economics of robotics.

Michael Abramov is the founder & CEO of Scryon, bringing over 15+ years of software engineering and computer vision AI systems experience to building enterprise-grade labelling tools.

Michael began his career as a software engineer and R&D manager, building scalable data systems and managing cross-functional engineering teams. Until 2025, he has served as the CEO of Keymakr, a data labelling service company, where he pioneered human-in-the-loop workflows, advanced QA systems, and bespoke tooling to support large-scale computer vision and autonomy data needs.

According to recent reports, he holds a B.Sc. in Computer Science and a background in engineering and creative arts, bringing a multidisciplinary lens to solving hard problems. Michael lives at the intersection of technology innovation, strategic product leadership, and real-world impact, driving forward the next frontier of autonomous systems and intelligent automation.

Breaking: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

In a recent development, you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

In a recent development, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

In a recent development, every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

It has been revealed that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The fresh Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

It has been revealed that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Recent findings suggest that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

In a recent development, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them upcoming paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Sources indicate that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Sources indicate that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

In a recent development, once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

According to recent reports, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#115301. Guilherme Joventino, Co-Founder & COO of MIGNOW – Interview Series

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2536 w)
